simple: a promise about speed that a test can check.
analogy: "20 °C in the living room at −10 °C outside with the door opened 30 times an hour", not "warm".
precise: in this course, a statement that names (1) the statistic (mean, or a percentile such as p99), (2) the threshold with its unit, (3) the offered load at which it must hold, (4) how that load is generated (open or closed loop), (5) the point where time is measured, and (6) the window over which the statistic is computed. A statement missing any part has a verdict that depends on a guess (Listing 2, R2) . This six-part checklist is the course's convention, built from the measurement protocol of curriculum 13.4 and the SLO definitions of F5-42 .
source: F12-11 (this build: own simulations budget.cpp and reqcheck.cpp; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many requests per second arrive at the system, whether it keeps up or not.
analogy: how often the front door opens, decided by the children, not by the heater.
precise: the arrival rate imposed on the system under test, in requests per second, as opposed to the throughput it actually completes. Below saturation the two are equal on average; above it, throughput stops growing while offered load keeps arriving and queues grow.
source: F12-11 (this build: own simulations budget.cpp and reqcheck.cpp; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an open-loop tester sends requests on a timetable; a closed-loop tester waits for each answer before sending the next.
analogy: children who open the door whenever they like, versus one child who waits until the room is warm again before going out.
precise: an open-loop generator issues requests at times fixed in advance (for example exponential gaps at rate λ), independent of the system's responses; a closed-loop generator has a fixed number of clients, each sending its next request only after the previous reply. A closed-loop test with one client never builds a queue, so it cannot observe queueing delay (Listing 2, R2; the measurement consequences are the subject of F12-13) .
source: F12-11 (this build: own simulations budget.cpp and reqcheck.cpp; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the total time a request may take, divided into parts, one per piece of the system.
analogy: 60 days for the house: 10 for the foundation, 20 for walls, 15 for the roof, 15 inside.
precise: an allocation of an end-to-end latency target to the components on the request's critical path, each owned by a team, such that meeting every component's allocation implies meeting the end-to-end target. Allocations of means add exactly; allocations of percentiles do not (Listing 1, R1) .
source: F12-11 (this build: own simulations budget.cpp and reqcheck.cpp; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when one request waits for many smaller ones, it is slow whenever any one of them is slow.
analogy: the house is late if any one of ten deliveries is late.
precise: if a request waits for k independent calls and each call exceeds its own p99 with probability 0.01, the request meets at least one such slow call with probability 1 − 0.99k (arithmetic of independent events; checked by simulation in R1) ; the effect in large services is discussed in D5 .
source: F12-11 (this build: own simulations budget.cpp and reqcheck.cpp; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a test that fails when the system is too slow.
analogy: the inspector's thermometer in the living room on a cold evening.
precise: an executable check that measures a performance requirement under its stated conditions and compares the result with a target that was written down before the work began; curriculum 13.4 adds that targets are never lowered afterwards without the owner's explicit approval and a log entry .
source: F12-11 (this build: own simulations budget.cpp and reqcheck.cpp; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small calculation that predicts how fast a system will be, made before you measure it.
analogy: Yusuf's envelope: bricks, bricklayers, the mixer, the expected days.
precise: a simplified quantitative description of a system (its resources, the work each request demands of them, and the arrival pattern) from which throughput and latency can be predicted; it states its assumptions so that a measurement can confirm or refute it. Families used in this university: operational laws, queueing models, the roofline model (F2-56), the alpha–beta model (F1-62) and Amdahl's law (F2-34) .
source: F12-12 (this build: own simulations queue_model.cpp, lockmodel.cpp and the measured predict_real.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Harchol-Balter's queueing textbook, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long one request keeps a resource busy.
analogy: ten minutes of the mixer per bucket.
precise: the service time S of a resource is the time it is busy with one request (excluding waiting); the service demand of a request at a resource is the total of its service times there. Latency = waiting time + service time.
source: F12-12 (this build: own simulations queue_model.cpp, lockmodel.cpp and the measured predict_real.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Harchol-Balter's queueing textbook, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how busy a resource is equals how many requests per second it finishes times how long each takes.
analogy: four buckets an hour × ten minutes = forty minutes of mixing per hour: busy two thirds of the time.
precise: U = X × S, where X is the completion rate and S the mean service time; it follows from the definitions (busy time / elapsed time = completions × mean service time / elapsed time) and needs no assumption about distributions . Compare utilisation of an RTOS task set (OS305).
source: F12-12 (this build: own simulations queue_model.cpp, lockmodel.cpp and the measured predict_real.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Harchol-Balter's queueing textbook, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the resource that fills up first as load grows.
analogy: the one mixer, if the bricklayers could otherwise go faster.
precise: the resource with the largest service demand per request, Dmax; because its utilisation cannot exceed 1, the system's throughput is bounded by X ≤ 1 / Dmax (for a resource with c identical servers, X ≤ c / D) .
source: F12-12 (this build: own simulations queue_model.cpp, lockmodel.cpp and the measured predict_real.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Harchol-Balter's queueing textbook, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a mathematical picture of requests waiting in line for a server.
analogy: bricklayers arriving at the mixer at random moments and waiting their turn.
precise: in Kendall's notation, A/B/c names the arrival process, the service-time distribution and the number of servers; M means memoryless (Poisson arrivals or exponential service times), D means deterministic (constant); "M/M/1" is Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server, served first come first served .
source: F12-12 (this build: own simulations queue_model.cpp, lockmodel.cpp and the measured predict_real.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Harchol-Balter's queueing textbook, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: work waiting because a resource is already busy.
analogy: the line of bricklayers at the mixer.
precise: the degree to which a resource has more work than it can serve at once, observed as queue length, waiting time or blocked threads; it grows sharply as utilisation approaches 1. Gregg's USE method checks utilisation, saturation and errors for every resource (F12-14) . Not the same as sensor saturation (MA202) or actuator saturation (RB202).
source: F12-12 (this build: own simulations queue_model.cpp, lockmodel.cpp and the measured predict_real.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Harchol-Balter's queueing textbook, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the written rules of a speed test, decided before you run it.
analogy: "same wall, alternate mornings and afternoons, ten tries each, the middle time decides".
precise: the specification of a benchmark run: question and prediction, workload, environment and its record, warm-up, number and order of repetitions, statistic, interval method and decision rule. Curriculum 13.4's protocol (warm-up runs, then the median of at least 20 timed runs, settings recorded, reference measured by the same harness) is the minimum used in this university .
source: F12-13 (this build: own simulations omission.cpp, bootstrap.cpp, drift.cpp and the measured ab_bench.cc; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", Jain, "The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis", Efron and Tibshirani, "An Introduction to the Bootstrap", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the point after which the system's speed has stopped changing because it has "settled in".
analogy: after the first wheelbarrow, when the boards are laid and the mortar is mixed.
precise: the regime in which the measured statistic no longer drifts with time: caches, memory pages, just-in-time compilation, connection pools, queue lengths and device clocks have reached their running condition. Warm-up runs (F2-51) aim to reach it; for a service under load, the first minutes of a run are usually discarded for the same reason.
source: F12-13 (this build: own simulations omission.cpp, bootstrap.cpp, drift.cpp and the measured ab_bench.cc; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", Jain, "The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis", Efron and Tibshirani, "An Introduction to the Bootstrap", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: taking turns between the two things you compare, instead of doing all of one and then all of the other.
analogy: alternating the two bricklaying methods morning and afternoon, so the rain falls on both.
precise: an ordering of benchmark runs that alternates variants (here A B, then B A, and so on) so that slow changes of the machine (drift, background jobs, thermal state) affect both variants nearly equally, instead of being confused with the difference between them. It turns a time trend from a common cause (confounder) into noise.
source: F12-13 (this build: own simulations omission.cpp, bootstrap.cpp, drift.cpp and the measured ab_bench.cc; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", Jain, "The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis", Efron and Tibshirani, "An Introduction to the Bootstrap", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a range of plausible values for a result, found by re-drawing your own measurements many times.
analogy: shuffling the ten timing cards of each method, drawing ten with replacement, and seeing how much the middle time moves.
precise: a percentile-bootstrap interval resamples each variant's runs with replacement, recomputes the statistic (here the ratio of medians) for each resample, and reports the 2.5 % and 97.5 % points of those values as an approximate 95 % interval; it needs no assumption that times are normally distributed (Listing 2) .
source: F12-13 (this build: own simulations omission.cpp, bootstrap.cpp, drift.cpp and the measured ab_bench.cc; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", Jain, "The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis", Efron and Tibshirani, "An Introduction to the Bootstrap", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a load tester that waits for slow answers stops sending, so it never measures how long the requests it did not send would have waited.
analogy: timing deliveries from when the truck left the depot; while the depot is closed no truck leaves, so no delivery looks late.
precise: a measurement error of closed-loop load generators: when the system stalls, the generator delays its next requests (it is "coordinated" with the system) and times them from their late actual send, so the stall appears as one slow sample instead of as every request that should have been sent during it. Fixed by open-loop generation, or by timing from the intended send time (Listing 1) .
source: F12-13 (this build: own simulations omission.cpp, bootstrap.cpp, drift.cpp and the measured ab_bench.cc; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", Jain, "The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis", Efron and Tibshirani, "An Introduction to the Bootstrap", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: everything someone needs to rerun your test and check your number.
analogy: the contest sheet with dates, weather, bricks used and every try's time.
precise: the raw per-run data, the protocol, the code version, the build command, the toolchain version line, the machine (processor, core count, virtualisation, other load), relevant settings (clock frequency policy where controllable, affinity), date and the statistic with its interval; the run logs of this university record the same fields (AH-23) .
source: F12-13 (this build: own simulations omission.cpp, bootstrap.cpp, drift.cpp and the measured ab_bench.cc; Systems Curriculum 13.4; Gregg, "Systems Performance", Jain, "The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis", Efron and Tibshirani, "An Introduction to the Bootstrap", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a record of where every part of the system spent its time, collected together during one run.
analogy: Ingrid's cards on every wheelbarrow, plus the gatekeeper's diary and each worker's timesheet, for the same day.
precise: a set of time-aligned measurements of one run of a system under a defined load: per-request traces (where requests spent their time), per-thread or per-process resource use (CPU time, context switches), per-resource utilisation and saturation (locks, queues, disks, network) and an event log of background activity. It answers "where did the time go?" for the user-visible metric, not only "which function uses the CPU?"
source: F12-14 (this build: the measured, instrumented service kvsvc.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", title only; Linux and strace manual pages, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: time a thread spends running instructions, and time it spends waiting.
analogy: a bricklayer laying bricks, and the same bricklayer standing at the gate.
precise: a thread's wall-clock time divides into time scheduled on a processor (on-CPU) and time blocked or runnable but not running (off-CPU: waiting for a lock, I/O, a condition variable, a timer, or for a processor). A sampling profiler of CPU use sees only on-CPU time; off-CPU time is seen through tracing of blocking events, per-thread CPU time against wall time, context-switch counts and system-call timing .
source: F12-14 (this build: the measured, instrumented service kvsvc.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", title only; Linux and strace manual pages, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: for every resource, ask how busy it is, how much work waits for it, and whether it fails.
analogy: for the gate: how often is it closed or in use, how long is the queue in front of it, does anything get turned away?
precise: a checklist method attributed to Brendan Gregg: for each resource (processors, memory, disks, network, and software resources such as locks, queues and thread pools) check utilisation (fraction of time busy, or fraction of capacity used), saturation (extra work waiting, such as a queue length or wait time) and errors. It finds bottlenecks that function profiles miss because the waiting resource is not a CPU .
source: F12-14 (this build: the measured, instrumented service kvsvc.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", title only; Linux and strace manual pages, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chain of steps that decides when a request finishes.
analogy: the wheelbarrow's route: lorry, gate, wall; making the lorry faster does not help if the gate is shut.
precise: the sequence of spans, including waits, on which the request's completion depends; time removed from a span off the critical path does not shorten the request. In a service, waits for queues, locks and durable writes are often on the critical path even when no thread uses the CPU.
source: F12-14 (this build: the measured, instrumented service kvsvc.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", title only; Linux and strace manual pages, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long one thread keeps a lock before letting go.
analogy: how long the inspector keeps the gate closed.
precise: the time between acquiring and releasing a lock in one critical section; every thread that needs the lock during that time waits at least until the release. Long holds by rare operations (snapshots, compaction, resizing) produce tail latency for frequent operations even when the lock's average utilisation is low.
source: F12-14 (this build: the measured, instrumented service kvsvc.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", title only; Linux and strace manual pages, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: finding out which cause made the slowest requests slow.
analogy: sorting the wheelbarrow cards by total time and checking what the slowest have in common.
precise: the analysis that compares the slowest requests (for example the slowest 1 %) with the rest: which spans grow, which events overlap them in time, and how much more often than for an ordinary request. A cause is supported when the slow requests share it far more often than the others and a change that removes it removes the tail; a single coincidence in time is not enough.
source: F12-14 (this build: the measured, instrumented service kvsvc.cc; Gregg, "Systems Performance", title only; Linux and strace manual pages, title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a written answer to "how much hardware do we need, by when, and why?"
analogy: the hiring plan for next season's busiest week, with the sums shown.
precise: a document that turns a requirement (an SLO), a measured capacity per unit (from a load test) and a demand forecast (peak, growth, horizon) into a number of units with redundancy, lists the assumptions, and says when it must be revisited. Its central rule: plan for the peak that must meet the requirement, with the failures you accept, not for the average .
source: F12-15 (this build: capacity.cpp, usl.cpp, the measured scale.cc and outage.cpp; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Gunther, "Guerrilla Capacity Planning", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the most work per second one machine can take while still meeting the latency promise.
analogy: the pace at which a bricklayer's walls stay straight, not the fastest pace he can manage.
precise: the highest offered load at which a load test of one unit still meets the latency SLO (here p99 ≤ 25 ms), measured under the production request mix. It is below the throughput limit because queueing delay rises steeply as utilisation approaches 1 (F12-12); in Listing 1's model it is 75 % of the CPU capacity .
source: F12-15 (this build: capacity.cpp, usl.cpp, the measured scale.cc and outage.cpp; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Gunther, "Guerrilla Capacity Planning", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much busier the busiest time is than an average time.
analogy: the busiest week's bricks divided by an average week's.
precise: the ratio of the demand in a chosen peak window (busiest hour, busiest minute) to the average demand over a longer window (a day, a week). Plans built on averages fail by roughly this factor at peak; the right window is the shortest one over which the system cannot absorb an overload in its queues without breaking the SLO.
source: F12-15 (this build: capacity.cpp, usl.cpp, the measured scale.cc and outage.cpp; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Gunther, "Guerrilla Capacity Planning", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: spare capacity kept free on purpose.
analogy: the bricklayer you could put on the wall tomorrow if a foundation is ready early.
precise: the difference between the capacity that meets the SLO and the current or forecast demand, kept to absorb forecast errors, bursts shorter than the planning window, failures and the lead time needed to add capacity. Headroom is stated in the same units as demand (req/s) and with the assumptions it covers.
source: F12-15 (this build: capacity.cpp, usl.cpp, the measured scale.cc and outage.cpp; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Gunther, "Guerrilla Capacity Planning", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a formula for how throughput grows, stops growing and can even fall as you add workers.
analogy: more bricklayers help, until they queue at the one mixer (contention) and spend their time telling each other what they changed (coherency).
precise: X(N) = λN / (1 + σ(N − 1) + κN(N − 1)), with λ the throughput of one unit, σ the contention (serialised) fraction and κ the coherency (crosstalk) cost. With κ = 0 it reduces to Amdahl's law in throughput form; with κ > 0 it has a peak at N* = √((1 − σ)/κ) and falls beyond it. Attributed to Neil Gunther ; fitted in Listing 2.
source: F12-15 (this build: capacity.cpp, usl.cpp, the measured scale.cc and outage.cpp; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Gunther, "Guerrilla Capacity Planning", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far ahead a plan must look, and how long it takes to get more capacity.
analogy: hiring takes two months, so in March you plan for May.
precise: the horizon is the period a plan must cover; it must be at least the lead time to obtain and bring capacity into service (purchase, delivery, installation, configuration, testing; or quota and region limits in a cloud) plus the interval between plan reviews.
source: F12-15 (this build: capacity.cpp, usl.cpp, the measured scale.cc and outage.cpp; Gregg, "Systems Performance", and Gunther, "Guerrilla Capacity Planning", title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
